To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
oligonucleotide-based mutagenesis can be effectively used to introduce large insertions into the mammalian genome.

oligonucleotide-directed gene disruption is several hundred-fold more efficient in ES cells lacking MMR than in wild-type ES cells and that four-nucleotides insertions escape MMR and can be efficiently introduced in Msh2/MSH6-proficient but Msh2/ Msh3-defective ES cells.
compound mismatches are only partially suppressed by the MMR system and that larger insertions can be introduced in Msh2-deficient ES cells, which can be used for gene targeting.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new gene targeting methods and with the role of DNA mismatch repair in the prevention of gene targeting.
the development of a gene-targeting technology that is applicable to MMR-proficient ES cells.
the development of a new method for the generation of knockout ES cells and mice, which will be useful for the analysis of genes with essential functions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MMR system is a major obstacle to gene targeting by oligonucleotides.
the MMR system is not an obstacle to gene targeting in ES cells.
oligonucleotide-directed gene targeting can be effectively used in ES cells deficient for MMR proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MMR machinery is very effective in suppressing single-base substitutions, but is less effective in suppressing larger deletions and insertions.
oligonucleotide-based gene disruption is a powerful tool for the generation of gene-targeted mice, provided that the MMR status is taken into account.
the MMR system can be used for site-specific mutagenesis, but that the Msh2-Msh3 branch of MSH proteins is a bottleneck for the process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
oligonucleotide-based gene targeting is feasible in MMR-proficiency, but that Msh3-deficiency is a convenient way to increase the efficiency of oligonucleotide-induced mutations.
the MSH3 branch of MSH2-MSH3/MSH6-MutSalpha MMR is the main determinant of MMR-mediated suppression of large insertions and that this branch of MMR can be bypassed in Msh3-null cells.
Msh3-deficiency is a useful alternative to Msh2-deficiency for oligonucleotides-mediated gene disruption in mouse ES cells.
